item.title: Goals should be measurable
item.description:
If goals aren’t measurable, how will you know when you’ve accomplished what you set out to do?

See [[Goals should be S.M.A.R.T]]

item.title: Goals should have a clear outcome
item.description:
Without a clear outcome, you can’t measure or achieve them.

These are poorly defined goals and miss out on one of the more important outputs of a well-defined goal, being able to see whether the goal is worth doing.

See [[Goals should be S.M.A.R.T]]

item.title: Goals should have an expected end date
item.description:
Without a clear outcome, these are more like dreams and aspirations than goals.

See also [[Goals should be S.M.A.R.T]].

item.title: The goals were not goals to begin with
item.description:
Dreams taste and smell like goals, but dreams don’t have a target end date.

When it comes to tracking progress, whether it be career, health, personal development, or cleaning up your room. Goals have a few qualities they possess that other things don’t.

It can be hard to think of a goal on the spot. These principles help:

  • [[Goals should have a clear outcome]]
  • [[Goals should have an expected end date]]
  • [[Goals should be measurable]]
  • [[Goals should be S.M.A.R.T]]

item.title: Tracking routines
item.description:
[[You can’t optimise what you can’t see]].

Looking back

Previously set goals were always:

  • short lived,
  • too ambitious,
  • poorly defined,
  • or [[The goals were not goals to begin with|the goals aren’t goals to begin with]].

Looking ahead

Once my goal was well defined, I can measure and track it. I’d make goals that:

item.title: Goals should be S.M.A.R.T
item.description:
• Specific - concise title for accomplishment or contribution.
  • Measurable - Quantifiable, progress can be tracked easily.
  • Achievable - needs to be realistic targets.
  • Relevant - should contribute to broader, long term goals.
  • Time-bound - better if it has a clear start and end date.

item.title: Inclusive Language
item.description:
We live in a world, filled with all sorts of people. A history filled with combinations of unique upbringings, cultures, experiences, joys and sufferings.

How language fits into all of this

Words matter. They are used to convey ideas, tell stories, describe objects, grow communities, teach others, etc.

Words can be used for good:

  • to uplift,
  • to inspire,
  • to comfort,
  • to bring clarity.

Or bad:

item.title: Blaming the user
item.description:
The user is clearly at fault, not your software. Right?

This topic seems to come up often. Let’s break it down.

Why you might feel this way

If you work in the service industry, you might know the expression:

“The customer is always right.”

It’s painful to hear, especially when it comes from the customer’s mouth, or your boss, or your colleague. So when might this happen?

item.title: Back to square one
item.description:
For some astute followers (shoutout to Pigeon), you may have noticed the blog had changed in appearance. And yes, you are correct.

The dilemma

I encountered no major issues using GatsbyJS – an enjoyable framework to use. Finding myself gradually becoming more distracted by what it had to offer consumed more time than I wanted to spend. I became trapped and focused on looking at the shiny, instead of focusing more on what I wanted to do originally – start writing some content.

item.title: Putting the blog together
item.description:
I enjoy reading. And as much as I wanted to write something, I never got around to it. With that said, this first post will dive straight into the thick of it.

Thought Process

I want to write content that I believe would help future me, and also inspire and help others. And so, I will share my current work-in-progress journey, one purposed to involve little time in maintaining.

item.title: About
item.description:
Hi there!

Like many, I have lofty dreams and grand ambitions. I love the idea of what software could do, and enjoy solving problems, tweaking systems, and learning new things.

What is important, is not only what you do, but how you do it.

What you’ll find

Content includes:

  • ramblings,
  • previous thoughts (and mistakes),
  • processes
  • #TIL (today I learned) moments,
  • hobbies and achievements,
  • tooling & setup,
  • niche problems,
  • some philosophy,

Open source

Has provided me with experience and tools I use even now. I believe in contributing and giving back to the open-source community.
